title: Partner, platform or plumbing: who will banking customers trust to run their financial lives?
summary: As AI takes on more financial decisions, customer trust will become critical. Explore who customers will trust to manage their financial lives.
body_markdown:
Open your banking app today, regardless of which one, and it will wait for you to deliver an instruction. Transfer some money to a family member. Pay a bill. Freeze a card.


However sophisticated the app we use, we all know the drill: as the customer we decide what should happen – and our bank then asks us to authorise it.


With delegated banking things are set to change. It’s why we published our recent white paper, *From Digital Banking to Delegated Banking: The Three Uncomfortable Truths About What Customers Will Choose by 2035* .


Instead of approving one action at a time, customers articulate a desired outcome. It could help to balance a monthly budget, build a rainy-day fund, or save towards a deposit.


The technology will then work continuously towards that objective, within limits the customer has agreed. It could transform financial services from something customers repeatedly interact with, into a capability quietly working on their behalf.


The technology required is already here. AI can interpret data and make recommendations. Automation can carry them out. Connected data can provide a broader, more current view of someone’s finances.


In this article we’re going to look at why capability isn’t the hardest part. The hard part is going to be earning the trust of delegated banking customers.


## **Less banking = more work?**


Delegated banking promises less effort: less reactive checking and approving, whilst noticing (sometimes too late) that your spending has crept upwards.


But there is a paradox here too. Customers might get to spend less time making individual financial decisions but… they will have to dedicate time instead to defining their goals, preferences and boundaries.


“Help me reduce my debt” might sound simple. In practice, it contains multitudes. Should the system prioritise the most expensive borrowing, or preserve an emergency buffer? How aggressively should it move money? What happens when circumstances change?


Where a skilled human adviser can hear an imprecise ambition, ask questions and help a customer understand the trade-offs, AI will need sufficiently clear instructions and guardrails in place to be able to do the same.


Organisations providing delegated banking will need to turn intentions into clear choices – ones that people genuinely understand. They must be able to explain the likely consequences and offer different degrees of delegation.


One customer may want recommendations only. Another may permit automatic transfers below an agreed limit. Both may want the technology to stop and involve a person when the decision carries greater risk.


## **Who gets the permission?**


The obvious assumption is that customers will delegate these decisions to their bank. That’s possible, but far from certain.


If the customer has an AI assistant it could potentially operate across several current accounts, savings products, investments, pensions and credit providers. Because it sees the entirety of a customer’s financial life, it may be better placed to coordinate it. That assistant might come from an existing platform such as Apple, Google or PayPal. Or it may come from an entirely new kind of trusted financial intermediary.


We’ve seen this happen elsewhere. Hotels own the rooms and deliver the stay, but platforms such as Booking.com often own the search, comparison and customer relationship. Banking could experience its own version of that hardware/software division. The bank might hold the deposits, provide the loan and carry the regulatory responsibility, while another organisation becomes the place where the customer makes – or delegates – their choices.


Would you give Google or Apple permission to interpret and execute your financial intentions? This isn’t simply about whether its systems are secure: trust is also about perception.


A technology platform like Google may already know an extraordinary amount about what someone searches for, where they travel, what’s in their calendar and how they spend their time. All that context could make its recommendations more intelligent. It could also leave customers wondering where the boundary lies. The same data that makes a service useful can make it feel intrusive.


Banks begin from a different position. They provide regulated products, protect financial assets and operate under strict requirements covering identity, financial crime and customer treatment. Customers know exactly who is responsible when something goes wrong. But many banks also have a narrower view of the customer, fragmented data and technology estates that make coordinated action difficult.


Technology platforms may be stronger in engagement, intelligence and customer experience. Banks are stronger in regulated financial services, risk and accountability. Neither possesses the whole answer.


## **Partner, platform or plumbing?**


This leaves banks with a strategic choice. They can build the complete delegated-banking experience themselves. They can assemble it through partnerships. Or they can allow somebody else to own the experience while they provide the regulated infrastructure underneath it.


Building everything in-house risks turning every bank into a technology company that must build, maintain and continually improve its own AI ecosystem. Partnering can bring capability more quickly, but raises difficult questions about data, control and ownership of the customer relationship.


The greatest danger may be failing to choose. In this scenario, a bank can remain essential to the transaction but become almost invisible to the customer. Once another platform holds the customer’s goals, permissions and everyday attention, it may also gatekeep which products are offered for consideration, when money moves and whether the customer stays with their provider.


Partnership doesn’t remove accountability. If automation makes a damaging decision – let’s say your AI agent goes rogue and invests your money in a yacht you never signed off on, who is responsible? The bank, the AI provider, the platform controlling the interface or the customer who nodded through the original instruction?


Real examples will be less entertaining and more painful: a legitimate payment stopped, savings moved at the wrong moment, or an unsuitable product selected. Customers will expect an explanation, the ability to challenge the decision and a person with the authority to put it right.


## **Trust is the real product**


Not every customer will delegate in the same way. Someone may happily allow £20 to be swept into savings but insist on personally approving anything affecting their mortgage. Comfort levels will differ and change with life experience and circumstance.


Delegation must therefore be progressive, adjustable and reversible. Customers need visible boundaries and an easy route back to human help. Humans will be needed to clarify intentions, supervise AI agents, manage exceptions and accept accountability when judgement is required.


Ultimately the winner in delegated banking will be the one customers trust to act in their interests. That could be a bank. It could be a technology platform. It could be a new intermediary… or a partnership combining the strengths of all three.


Banking has spent decades asking customers to authorise what should happen next. Its next era may begin by asking what they are trying to achieve. Whoever earns the right to act on that answer could become the true orchestrator of the customer’s financial life.
